722.title: Athanasius (c. 296–373)
722.hook: exiled again and again, he held that Christ is truly God
722.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Athanasius as a bishop and Doctor of the Church, and his teaching that the Son is one in being with the Father is professed in the Creed at Sunday Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pachomius, the soldier who gathered monks under one wall and one rule. Your line was together in the desert.

Night, in a church in Alexandria. The people are keeping vigil with their bishop. Soldiers surround the building, and then they break in. In his own account, the bishop doesn't bolt for the back door. He stays in his chair. He tells the deacon to begin a psalm, and the people answer the refrain, for his mercy endureth for ever, while they slip out ahead of him. Only when most are safe does he slip away himself, into the dark. His name is Athanasius, and it isn't the first time he's had to run.
screen: `SOLDIERS AT THE DOORS.` → `HE STAYS IN HIS CHAIR.` → `THE PSALM KEEPS GOING.`

segments.voice: First, who he was: bishop of Alexandria, a great city of the early Church, when emperors took a close interest in what bishops taught. Athanasius held one thing with his whole life: that Jesus Christ, the Son, is truly God, not the highest of creatures but one in being with the Father. Tomorrow, the argument on the other side. Second, what it cost him. Emperors sent him away, and sent him away again, to distant cities. He hid in the desert among the monks, who kept him safe, and, tradition says, once in his own father's tomb. Each time he came back and took up his work, writing letters and books from wherever he was. Third, why it mattered to him. In his little book On the Incarnation, he gives the reason in a single sentence: "He was made man that we might be made God." If the Son were only a creature, Athanasius argued, he couldn't join us to God, because he would be on our side of the line too. Only God could bring us to God. The Catechism of the Catholic Church still quotes that line. Fourth, the phrase in today's carry. Later generations summed him up in Latin: Athanasius contra mundum, Athanasius against the world. It's a saying about him, not a slogan he chose, and it can be misheard as stubbornness for its own sake. For Athanasius, the point was never to win. It was to keep handing on what the Church had confessed, even when it was unpopular, even when it meant sleeping in the desert. Catholics honor him as a saint and a Doctor of the Church.

segments.voice: Think of something you hold to be true, about faith, fairness or a person, that you don't say out loud because it would cost you a little. Don't rehearse an argument; ask a gentler question: what would it look like to stand by this, kindly, without needing to win? If you pray, ask for courage and gentleness together.
Athanasius. The bishop of Alexandria who, through exile after exile, held that Christ is truly God. Today's word.

723.title: The Arian question
723.hook: was there a time when the Son was not? A priest's popular songs spread the answer no
723.howItsDone: At Sunday Mass Catholics profess the Creed, which says the Son is one in being with the Father, a teaching from the Council of Nicaea that Catholic, Orthodox and other churches share.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Athanasius, sent into exile again and again and coming back each time. Your line was athanasius against the world.

Down by the harbor in Alexandria, people are singing theology. Tradition says a priest named Arius put his teaching into catchy verse, and that sailors and millers and travelers picked up the songs and carried them on. Set to a tune, a hard question goes a long way. Was there a time when the Son of God was not? Arius's songs gave one answer. His bishop, and a deacon named Athanasius, gave the other. And the argument filled the streets.
screen: `THEOLOGY BY THE HARBOR.` → `A PRIEST'S CATCHY SONGS.` → `WAS THERE A TIME?`

segments.voice: First, Arius's side, put fairly. He honored the Son highly. The Son, he taught, was made by the Father before anything else, and through him the world was made. But made: a creature, the first and greatest, not eternal like the Father. So his followers could say: there was when he was not. It sounded reverent and simple, and it protected the idea that God is one. Second, the reply. Bishop Alexander, and Athanasius after him, went back to the opening of John's Gospel. In the Douay-Rheims: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Not became. Was. If the Son is a creature, they said, Christians are worshipping a creature. That was the stake: not a word game, but who Jesus is. Third, the word that decided it. A council of bishops gathered at Nicaea under Constantine. They wrote a creed, and chose a Greek word for the Son: homoousios, of one substance, one in being with the Father. The creed said at Sunday Mass grew out of that council and the councils after it. Fourth, how far the question went. Saint Gregory of Nyssa, writing later about Constantinople, joked about it. Ask a man in the market for change, he wrote, and he gives you a lecture on the begotten and the unbegotten. Ask the price of bread, and you're told the Father is greater and the Son is less. Ask if the bath is ready, and you hear that the Son was made from nothing. The question of the age had reached the bakery and the bathhouse.

segments.voice: In Matthew, after hearing what everyone else says about him, Jesus turns to his disciples: "But whom do you say that I am?" Let the question sit, without needing the right answer or any answer, and notice what comes up first, and what comes after. If you pray, bring whatever answer you have, or don't have, to God; if not, let the question keep you company.

Your line: the question of the age. It's still asked today. Day seven hundred twenty-three, done.

724.title: Basil's city of mercy
724.hook: Basil builds a complex of hospitals and hostels outside Caesarea
724.howItsDone: Catholic parishes, religious orders and charities run hospitals, shelters and food programs, and Catholics often volunteer in them as one of the corporal works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Arian question, and the word homoousios, sung by the harbor and argued over the price of bread. Your line was the question of the age.

Outside the walls of Caesarea, in Cappadocia, something is going up that isn't a palace. Rooms for travelers passing through. Rooms for the sick. Houses for the people who nurse them, workshops, a church. And space for the people the town would rather not see at all: the lepers. Someone has already complained about it to the governor, and the builder means to answer. The man behind it is Basil, the city's bishop.
screen: `OUTSIDE THE WALLS.` → `ROOMS FOR TRAVELERS AND THE SICK.` → `A NEW CITY.`

segments.voice: First, what it was. Not one hospital, but a cluster of buildings with a single purpose: to take in whoever needed taking in. The stranger on the road. The sick with no family to nurse them. The poor. Gregory, in the speech he gave after Basil's death, tells his listeners to walk out a little way from the city and look at it. He calls it a new city, a storehouse of godliness, where sickness is seen in the light of faith and compassion is put to the test. Second, a letter. Someone had spoken against the project to the governor. Basil wrote back. Who is harmed, he asks, by a church for God, a house for the bishop, and rooms around it for guests and travelers, for those who need care, for the nurses and doctors and workers who serve them? He lets the list speak. Third, his hands. Gregory says Basil didn't run the place from a distance. He went to the lepers himself, greeted them, embraced them, treated them as brothers, and urged the well-off to do the same, so that people would stop avoiding them. Gregory saw Christ honored in the very people others turned away. Fourth, why it lasted. Mercy here wasn't a mood or a single kind deed. It had walls and a roof and a staff. It would still be there tomorrow. Catholic hospitals, hostels and shelters carry the same idea: mercy given a building, so it doesn't depend on anyone's good day.

segments.voice: Picture the places near you that take people in: a shelter, a food pantry, a hospital, a parish kitchen, a home for the elderly. Let one come to the front, its door and the people behind it, and stay there a moment. If you pray, pray for the people who work there and the people they care for.
Basil's city of mercy. The rooms for travelers, the sick and the lepers that Basil built outside Caesarea, which Gregory called a new city. Today's word.
Your line: a city of mercy. Kindness, given walls and a roof so it lasts. Until tomorrow.

725.title: The bread you keep
725.hook: Basil preached that bread you hoard belongs to the hungry
725.howItsDone: Catholic parishes often keep food collection boxes and run pantries, and Catholic social teaching speaks of the universal destination of goods: owning something carries a duty to people in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Basil's new city outside Caesarea, with rooms for travelers, the sick and the lepers. Your line was a city of mercy.

"I will pull down my barns, and will build greater." That's a rich man talking to himself in one of Jesus's parables in Luke. His land has brought in a huge harvest, more than his storage can hold. So he makes a plan: bigger barns, then rest, eat, drink, be merry. That same night, God tells him his life will be required of him, and asks whose all that grain will be now. Basil preached a whole sermon on that one sentence, and he started by counting the rich man's pronouns.
screen: `A HARVEST TOO BIG.` → `BIGGER BARNS.` → `THAT SAME NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, Basil listens to the rich man's words. My fruits. My barns. My goods. My soul. He talks only to himself. He doesn't ask anyone. He doesn't look up from the pile. And Basil asks the question underneath: what is actually yours? You came into the world with nothing, and you'll leave with nothing. Second, a picture from his city. Imagine, Basil says, someone who gets to the theater early, takes a seat, and then tries to keep everyone else out, as if a show meant for everyone belonged to him because he arrived first. That, he says, is what the rich do with what was given for all: they grab it first and then call it theirs. Third, the line that gives today its name. Basil says it plainly to his congregation. The bread you are keeping belongs to the hungry. The coat you have stored away belongs to the one who has none. The shoes going to waste in your house belong to the barefoot. The money you have buried belongs to the one in need. He's not saying a barn is evil, or that having things is a sin. He's saying the extra, the part sitting idle while someone goes without, already has an owner. Fourth, why Catholics still read him. Catholic teaching speaks of the universal destination of goods: the things of the earth are meant for everyone, and owning something carries a duty toward the people who need it. Basil's sermon said something close to it long before. Read that way, a barn can be a freezer, a pantry, a closet.

726.title: Two Gregorys and a friendship
726.hook: Gregory of Nazianzus and Basil, friends since student days
726.howItsDone: The Catholic Church keeps the memorial of Saints Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen together on one day, honoring the two friends side by side.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Basil on the rich man's barns: the bread you keep belongs to the hungry. Your line was the hungry own it.

Athens, a city full of schools, and full of students who like to make newcomers miserable. Two young men from Cappadocia are there to study. One is Basil. The other is Gregory, whose family was from Nazianzus. Gregory, by his own account, stepped in to spare Basil the usual treatment new arrivals got. A favor between students. It turned into the friendship of their lives. And there's a second Gregory in this story too.
screen: `ATHENS, A CITY OF SCHOOLS.` → `A FAVOR BETWEEN STUDENTS.` → `THE FRIENDSHIP OF THEIR LIVES.`

segments.voice: First, how Gregory describes it. After Basil died, Gregory gave a long speech in his honor, and that speech is where we hear about Athens. He says the two of them shared everything: lodgings, meals, studies, hopes. They seemed, he says, to have one soul living in two bodies. Second, the two roads. A great city has endless distractions, and Gregory says they knew only two roads: one to the churches and the teachers there, the other to their lessons. Feasts, shows and parties they left to others. Their friendship had a direction, and it was the same direction. Third, the crack. This friendship isn't painted as perfect. When Basil became a bishop, in the middle of a church dispute, he made Gregory bishop of a small town called Sasima. Gregory describes the place as a dusty, noisy crossroads. He felt used, and he said so to Basil, sharply. By his own telling, he never really took up the post. The friendship was badly strained. And yet the long speech of praise came from Gregory. He kept the friend, and told the truth about the wound. Fourth, the other Gregory. Basil had a younger brother, also named Gregory, who became bishop of Nyssa. You heard him a few days ago, joking about bread and theology. Basil, his brother Gregory of Nyssa, and his friend Gregory of Nazianzus are honored together as the Cappadocian Fathers. One Gregory, a friend who was like a brother; the other, a brother who became a friend in the faith. And two of them, as tomorrow will show, owed a great deal to their older sister.
screen: `ONE SOUL, TWO BODIES.` · `TWO ROADS ONLY.` · `THE TOWN CALLED SASIMA.` · `THE SECOND GREGORY.` · then, large: `ONE SOUL IN TWO BODIES.`

segments.voice: Let a face come to mind, someone who shared a room or a road or a hard year with you, whether you're still close or life pulled you apart. Remember one thing they gave you, a favor, a laugh, a word at the right time, and stay with it. If you pray, thank God for them by name.

727.title: Macrina the teacher
727.hook: Basil and Gregory of Nyssa's older sister taught them both
727.tomorrow: Ephrem, the harp of the Spirit (d. 373)
727.howItsDone: The Catholic Church honors Macrina as a saint, and Catholics who know her story often remember her alongside her brothers Basil and Gregory of Nyssa; Gregory's Life of Macrina is still read as spiritual reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two Gregorys and a friendship: Gregory of Nazianzus and Basil, friends since their student days. Your line was one soul in two bodies.

This story isn't flattering to Basil, the same Basil from yesterday. He has come home from his studies, trained as a public speaker, and he's good at it, and he knows it. Their younger brother Gregory, later bishop of Nyssa, wrote it down: Basil came back puffed up with his own eloquence, looking down on everyone. Waiting at home is his older sister. She has no famous teachers and no title. Her name is Macrina. And she set about turning him around.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN COMES HOME PROUD.` → `HIS OLDER SISTER IS WAITING.` → `SHE TURNS HIM AROUND.`

segments.voice: Macrina's story comes to us through her brother Gregory, in a short book called the Life of Macrina, so this is a portrait drawn by someone who loved her. He says she was taught at home, not in the schools, and that the Psalms went with her through the whole day: when she got up, worked, rested, ate, and went to bed. That's where her learning came from. When Basil came home proud, Gregory says, she drew him away from chasing a name for himself and toward a simple life given to God. Basil listened. Macrina didn't stop with her brother. He says she persuaded their mother to live on the same level as the women who had served them, so the household became a community of prayer and work, sharing one table. He says she also raised their youngest brother, Peter, almost as a mother would. Now the ending. Basil has died, and Gregory, heartbroken, travels to see his sister, and finds her dying too. She lets him grieve for a little while. Then she starts to teach. They talk about death, the soul and the resurrection, and afterward Gregory writes the conversation down as a dialogue. Look at how it's built. The famous bishop asks the questions, and his sister gives the answers. Through most of it he doesn't use her name. He calls her the Teacher. The Catholic Church honors Macrina as a saint, and her two pupils, Basil and Gregory, as saints too.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who taught you up close, not from a stage: an older sister, a grandmother, a coach, a teacher whose name you still remember. Macrina the teacher. The older sister of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, who taught them at home and at her deathbed, and whom her brother simply called the Teacher. Today's word.
Your line: the teacher of saints. Some of the best teachers never had a title. See you tomorrow.

728.title: Ephrem, the harp of the Spirit (d. 373)
728.hook: a Syriac deacon who taught theology through women's choirs and hymns
728.howItsDone: The Catholic Church honors Ephrem as a saint and a Doctor of the Church; Syriac Catholic, Maronite and Chaldean Catholics, among others, still pray in liturgies shaped by the Syriac tradition he wrote in.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Macrina the teacher, the older sister who turned Basil around and answered Gregory's questions at her deathbed. Your line was the teacher of saints.

What does a creed sound like when it's sung? Go east, past the Greek-speaking cities, to churches that pray in Syriac. A deacon there is rehearsing a choir. The singers are women. The songs are about the birth of Christ, the cross, paradise, the bread of the altar. Arguments about who Christ is are loud in these years, and hard to follow. This deacon's answer is not a longer argument. It's a rehearsal, verse by verse, until the women know it by heart. His name is Ephrem.
screen: `A CREED YOU CAN SING.` → `A DEACON AND A CHOIR OF WOMEN.` → `NOT AN ARGUMENT, A REHEARSAL.`

segments.voice: Ephrem was a deacon, not a bishop, and he wrote in Syriac, much of it in poems meant to be sung. A later Syriac poet, Jacob of Serugh, wrote a long sung homily in his honor. Jacob says Ephrem saw that the women of the church were kept silent, so he gathered them into choirs and taught them his hymns, and the women became teachers of the whole assembly. Doctrine, carried by women's voices, line by line. The letter to the Colossians asks for something like it. In the Douay-Rheims it speaks of "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual canticles." Ephrem's choirs come close to it. And notice how he does theology. When people wanted to dissect God, to pin down exactly how the Son is born of the Father, Ephrem pushed back in his hymns on faith. Some things, he says, are for praising, not for prying into. Across his hymns he turns to pictures instead: the pearl, the womb of Mary, the robe of light Adam lost and Christ gives back. Scripture and nature, for him, are full of signs pointing to God, and a hymn can hold a sign without flattening it. Tradition calls him the harp of the Spirit. The Catholic Church names him a Doctor of the Church, one of the teachers whose writing it holds up for everyone. For Ephrem, the hymn was the lesson, and the choir was the classroom.
screen: `A DEACON WHO WROTE IN SONG.` · `CHOIRS OF WOMEN TEACH THE CHURCH.` · `PRAISE, NOT PRYING.` · `A DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH.` · then, large: `THE HARP OF THE SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Find a hymn you know, a carol, a verse from Mass, something a grandmother hummed, and sing it quietly, even under your breath. Then listen to the words as if someone were teaching you with them: what do they say about God? If you don't know a hymn, hum any tune that's been sung in a church and notice what it does to your breathing.
Ephrem. A Syriac deacon who taught the faith in hymns and trained choirs of women to sing them. Tradition calls him the harp of the Spirit. Today's word.
Your line: theology you can sing. From Athanasius and the Arian question, through Basil's city of mercy, two Gregorys and Macrina, to a deacon with a choir. That's the week.
screen: `THIS WEEK: ATHANASIUS · BASIL · THE GREGORYS · MACRINA · EPHREM.`
